analysis.one_liner: Cuts the standard federal workweek to 32 hours, with overtime pay beyond that and beyond 8 hours a day.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee in March 2023, it never received a hearing or a vote, and drew 8 cosponsors, all Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the Fair Labor Standards Act so that employers owe overtime pay to most hourly workers after 32 hours in a week instead of 40, phased in over three years (38, 36, 34, then 32 hours). It would also require overtime pay after 8 hours in a single day and double pay after 12 hours. The bill would not force employers to cut hours — but it would make every hour beyond those limits cost at least 1.5 times normal pay, giving employers a strong reason to either raise take-home pay or schedule fewer hours per worker and hire more staff.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly workers who regularly work more than 32 hours a week or more than 8 hours a day — especially in retail, restaurants, warehouses, healthcare, and manufacturing. Workers putting in long shifts would earn overtime or double time they do not get today, and some workers could gain free time if employers re-balance schedules instead of paying overtime.

how_it_helps.text: The bill moves the overtime threshold from 40 hours a week down to 32 over three years, so hours 33-40 trigger at least time-and-a-half pay [S2][S3].
It creates a new daily overtime right: at least 1.5 times pay after 8 hours in a workday and double pay after 12 hours, which federal law does not require today [S2][S3].
It amends the Fair Labor Standards Act, the same law that established the 40-hour week and the federal minimum wage, extending its overtime protection to shorter schedules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with hourly workforces — large retailers, restaurant and hotel chains, warehouses, hospitals, and manufacturers — would face higher labor costs for schedules that run past 32 hours a week or 8 hours a day, or would need to hire more workers to cover the same hours. Some costs could pass to consumers through prices, and some workers could see scheduled hours cut as employers re-balance staffing.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies the shorter overtime thresholds to employers of every size, with no phase-in exemptions or small-business carve-out, which opponents could fairly call a steep one-size-fits-all cost increase for small employers [S3].

Employers are not required to keep weekly pay whole, so a worker whose hours are cut from 40 to 32 could see lower total pay unless market pressure or union contracts force make-up wages; hospitals, nursing homes, and other around-the-clock operations would face the largest staffing and cost pressures.

The daily overtime requirement (pay beyond 8 hours in a day) is stricter than many state laws and would complicate flexible scheduling arrangements such as four-day, ten-hour compressed weeks unless employers restructure pay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: workers who regularly work long weeks would either take home meaningfully more pay or gain hours of their lives back, while employers bear higher scheduling and labor costs and some workers could lose hours. The three-year phase-in gives employers time to adjust, but the lack of any small-business exemption and the absence of a guarantee that weekly pay stays whole are genuine design weaknesses an honest supporter should acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Takano introduced the bill on March 1, 2023, joined by Reps. Jayapal and Schakowsky as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day; that was the only action the bill ever received [S5].
Eight House Democrats cosponsored the bill in total; no House Republican and no senator signed on [S4].
The committee held no markup, hearing action, or floor vote on the bill through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with long-hours hourly workforces are better off: they avoid the higher overtime costs the bill would have imposed, and no schedule or pay changes were required of them.

industries.note: These industries run long-hour hourly schedules and would owe overtime after 32 hours a week and 8 hours a day, raising labor costs or forcing more hiring. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against the workers who would have gained pay or free time.

Around-the-clock staffing means many employees work shifts beyond 8 or 12 hours, so daily overtime and double-time rules would hit these employers hardest; the cost would fall on staffing budgets or prices.
These sectors commonly schedule 40-plus-hour weeks; the lower overtime threshold would raise the cost of existing schedules or push employers to spread hours across more workers.
